description:
ANTIGRAVITY Some machines on the Moon and Mars stopped working. Their stories didn't.

We’re curious builders, researchers, coders, and storytellers exploring the forgotten technology humans left on other worlds. We want to turn abandoned machines into stories that make people see space exploration differently.

The machines stopped. Our curiosity didn't.
summary:
### BEYOND THE LAST SIGNAL
*“A mission that refused to end”*  
**Team antigraviityyy | NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026**

For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we created **BEYOND THE LAST SIGNAL**, an interactive storytelling website about NASA's Mars rover, Opportunity (MER-B). Our aim was to bring its incredible journey to life and show why a rover that stopped communicating in 2018 is still worth remembering.

Instead of presenting its history as plain text, we built an 8-chapter interactive experience using authentic NASA images and mission data. It features an interactive 3D rover model with inspectable components, a map of its 45.16 km journey across Mars, scientific instrument diagrams, immersive sound effects and a quiz to test visitors' understanding.

The story follows Opportunity from its original 90-sol mission to an unexpected journey of almost 15 years. It covers its scientific discoveries, engineering challenges, remarkable survival and final days during the 2018 global dust storm.

We chose this challenge because we believe space exploration is not just about successful launches or new discoveries. It is also about the machines, people and stories behind those achievements.

Through this project, we want visitors to connect with Opportunity's journey and understand that although its mission has ended, its contribution to science and human exploration lives on.
details:
BEYOND THE LAST SIGNAL

“A mission that refused to end”

Team: antigraviityyy
Competition: NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026
Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars
Subject: Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity (MER-B / Oppy)
Deployment Platform: Netlify

1. Project Overview

When a space mission ends, the machine behind it is often remembered only through a few photographs, scientific reports and mission statistics. But what happens to the story of that machine? Does it become irrelevant just because it can no longer communicate with Earth?

This was the question behind BEYOND THE LAST SIGNAL, our project for the 2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge.

We chose NASA's Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity, popularly known as Oppy. Originally designed for a mission of just 90 Martian days (sols) and a driving distance of 600 metres, Opportunity went on to operate for 5,111 sols, almost 15 Earth years, and travelled 45.16 kilometres across the Martian surface.

We wanted to tell this story in a way that goes beyond reading dates and scientific achievements. Instead of creating another information-based website, we built an interactive, cinematic storytelling experience where visitors can follow Opportunity's journey, explore its engineering, understand its discoveries and experience the events that led to its final communication.

Our central idea is that a mission ending does not mean its story has to end.

2. What Does the Project Do?

BEYOND THE LAST SIGNAL is a single-page interactive website built around an eight-chapter chronological story. As visitors scroll through the website, they follow Opportunity's journey from its preparation on Earth to its final days on Mars.

Each chapter focuses on an important moment in the mission:

  1. The Last Signal: The final days of Opportunity during the 2018 global dust storm.
  2. A 90-Day Promise: Its construction, launch and dramatic landing inside Eagle Crater.
  3. The Clue in the Rocks: The discovery of Martian blueberries and evidence of ancient liquid water.
  4. Trapped on Another World: The Purgatory Dune incident, when all six wheels became trapped in soft sand.
  5. The Marathoner of Mars: Its journey across the Martian surface and remarkable scientific achievements.
  6. The Great Dark: How the massive dust storm blocked sunlight and left Opportunity without enough power.
  7. The Vigil: NASA's attempts to re-establish communication through more than 1,000 recovery commands.
  8. The First Planetary Heritage Site: What Opportunity's legacy means for future explorers and the preservation of human-made objects on other worlds.

The experience combines real NASA photographs, mission information, technical explanations and interactive elements to make the story accessible to both space enthusiasts and people who are discovering Opportunity for the first time.

3. Interactive Features

We wanted visitors to do more than simply scroll through a story. Several features are progressively unlocked as they explore different chapters.

A. Interactive 3D Opportunity Rover

We created an interactive 3D model of Opportunity using Three.js. Visitors can rotate the rover, zoom in and explore its different components.

The model includes interactive hotspots explaining important engineering systems:

  • Solar Arrays: Their role in generating electrical power.
  • Pancam Camera Assembly: Used for imaging the Martian landscape.
  • Robotic Arm: Carries scientific instruments used to examine rocks and soil.
  • Rocker-Bogie Suspension: The six-wheel suspension system that helped the rover navigate difficult terrain.

The idea is to give visitors a better understanding of the engineering behind a rover that survived far longer than originally expected.

B. Scientific Instruments Explorer

Opportunity carried several scientific instruments that helped researchers study the Martian surface.

Our interactive instrument section introduces visitors to its Athena science payload, including:

  • Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometer (APXS)
  • Mössbauer Spectrometer
  • Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT)
  • Miniature Thermal Emission Spectrometer (Mini-TES)
  • Microscopic Imager
  • Panoramic Camera (Pancam)

Each instrument has a specific role in understanding the composition and characteristics of Martian rocks and soil.

C. Interactive Mars Traverse Map

Opportunity travelled approximately 45.16 kilometres during its mission. We created an interactive map to help visitors understand the scale of this journey.

It highlights important locations along the rover's route, including Eagle Crater, Endurance Crater, Purgatory Dune, Victoria Crater, Santa Maria Crater and Perseverance Valley.

Instead of presenting the distance as just a number, the map helps visitors see how far the rover actually travelled.

D. Mission Debrief Quiz

At the end of the experience, visitors unlock a mission quiz containing questions about Opportunity's history, engineering, scientific discoveries and the decisions made during its mission.

The quiz provides instant feedback and explanations, making it a final learning experience rather than just a score-based activity.

E. Additional Interactive Elements

We also developed several elements to make the overall experience more immersive:

  • Mission HUD: A persistent interface inspired by spacecraft monitoring systems, displaying mission information and progress.
  • Mission Clock: Displays Earth time alongside mission-related information.
  • Telemetry Indicators: Visual elements inspired by communication systems and mission monitoring.
  • Progress Tracking: An eight-segment progress indicator that follows the visitor through the chapters.
  • Progressive Unlocks: Four interactive modules become available as visitors reach specific points in the story.

4. Sound Design and Immersion

Sound was an important part of our storytelling approach. We wanted the website to feel less like a conventional webpage and more like an experience of following a mission from Earth.

Instead of relying on external audio files, we used the browser's native Web Audio API to generate sounds directly.

Our sound system includes:

  • Martian Wind: Generated ambient background noise to create the atmosphere of the Martian surface.
  • Communication Pings: Short electronic tones inspired by signals from the Deep Space Network.
  • Unlock Sounds: Musical chimes that play when visitors unlock new interactive features.

The sound system is optional and can be controlled through the website interface.

5. What Makes This Project Different?

Our approach was to combine technical information with storytelling rather than treating them as two separate things.

A conventional educational website might tell visitors that Opportunity operated for almost 15 years. We wanted them to understand what that actually meant: surviving harsh winters, getting trapped in sand, dealing with mechanical problems and continuing to explore despite all these challenges.

Some of our key creative decisions include:

A mission-control-inspired interface: Instead of a traditional blog layout, we designed the website around a tactical mission console. The interface gives visitors the feeling of following a real space mission.

Storytelling through real NASA material: We used authentic NASA archival photographs and mission information to keep the experience connected to the actual events.

Progressive exploration: The four interactive modules are unlocked as visitors move through the story. This connects learning with exploration and gives visitors a reason to continue.

Science combined with emotion: We present the engineering and scientific facts alongside the human effort behind them. Opportunity's story is also the story of the engineers and scientists who spent years keeping it operational.

Procedural audio: Generating sound directly through JavaScript allowed us to create an atmospheric experience without depending on external audio files.

6. Benefits of the Project

We believe the project offers value in several ways:

1. Making Space Science Accessible: Technical mission reports can be difficult for general audiences. Our interactive storytelling format presents the same subject in a more approachable way.

2. Encouraging Curiosity: The 3D rover, instrument explorer and traverse map allow visitors to explore the engineering and science behind the mission.

3. Preserving Space Exploration Stories: The project gives attention to a mission that might otherwise be remembered only through its final communication and scientific results.

4. Supporting Education: The website can be used by students, educators and space enthusiasts to learn about planetary exploration.

5. Promoting Open Science: By using NASA's publicly available photographs and mission information, we also encourage visitors to explore the original sources themselves.

7. Intended Impact

The main idea behind the NASA challenge is to think about what happens to human-made equipment when its mission ends on another world.

As space exploration expands, more spacecraft, landers and rovers will eventually stop operating on the Moon and Mars. These objects are not simply pieces of machinery. They represent important moments in the history of exploration.

Through Opportunity's story, we want to encourage people to look at these objects differently.

Our project highlights three important ideas:

  • Space Heritage Preservation: Recognising historic spacecraft and exploration sites as important parts of human history.
  • Scientific Awareness: Showing how publicly available NASA data can be used to create meaningful educational experiences.
  • Inspiring Future Explorers: Introducing younger audiences to the engineering, problem-solving and scientific curiosity behind planetary missions.

We also explore the possibility of future astronauts visiting these historic locations and seeing the machines that first helped humanity understand other worlds.

8. Technologies Used

We built the website using standard web technologies, keeping the application lightweight and accessible.

Technology

Purpose

Website structure and content

Interactivity and application logic

Development Environment:

  • Visual Studio Code
  • Windows 11
  • PowerShell
  • Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge

The application uses vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript rather than relying on a large frontend framework. This keeps the project relatively lightweight and avoids requiring a complicated build process.

9. Factors We Considered During Development

While building the project, we had to balance several things.

Scientific Accuracy: Since this is a NASA-related project, we wanted the story to remain connected to actual mission events and publicly available information. We used NASA archival material and mission records as the foundation for the narrative.

User Experience: An interface can look futuristic but still become difficult to read. We paid attention to text contrast, navigation, chapter structure and responsive layouts.

Performance: We wanted the website to work across different devices, including smartphones and lower-powered computers. This influenced our decision to use lightweight web technologies.

Accessibility: We kept the sound system optional and designed the interface to work through ordinary web browsers without requiring additional plugins.

Respect for the Mission: We did not want to present Opportunity's final days as just another technological failure. Its mission lasted far beyond its original expectations, and its final resting place represents an important chapter in the history of planetary exploration.

10. Our Conclusion

Opportunity was sent to Mars with an expected lifetime of just 90 sols. It continued working for 5,111 sols, travelling 45.16 kilometres and making discoveries that changed our understanding of the planet.

For us, this project was about more than creating an interactive website. It was about finding a way to tell a story that deserved to be remembered.

Behind every kilometre travelled was an engineering decision. Behind every discovery was a scientific question. And behind every communication received from Mars were people on Earth waiting for a signal.

BEYOND THE LAST SIGNAL is our tribute to Opportunity and to everyone who made its extraordinary journey possible.

Its last signal may have reached Earth in 2018, but its story is still travelling.
